title: Mastering kubectl
description: Learn essential kubectl commands for inspecting, debugging, and managing Kubernetes clusters.

data.text: `kubectl` (abbreviated as `k`) is the command-line tool for interacting with Kubernetes clusters. You use it to deploy applications, inspect resources, debug issues, and manage the cluster lifecycle.
The general syntax is: `kubectl [command] [type] [name] [flags]`. Most commands follow the pattern: `kubectl <verb> <resource> <name-or-yaml>`.

terms.definition: A configuration group that includes a cluster, user, and namespace — `kubectl config use-context` switches between them.
A virtual partition inside a cluster that isolates resources — useful for separating environments or teams.
An endpoint in the Kubernetes API that represents a cluster object like a Pod, Service, or Deployment.

data.title: Getting and describing resources
data.content: View cluster resources at different levels of detail.
data.code:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl get deploy,svc
kubectl get all -o wide
kubectl describe pod nginx-deployment-abc123

data.caption: Typical workflow when using kubectl to inspect resources.

cards.title: get
cards.description: Lists resources in a compact table format.

cards.title: describe
cards.description: Shows detailed information about a single resource, including events.

cards.title: logs
cards.description: Streams stdout/stderr from a container in a Pod.

items: `-n` or `--namespace` — Scope the command to a specific namespace.
`-o` or `--output` — Format output (yaml, wide, json, jsonpath).

data.title: Applying and deleting manifests
data.content: The standard workflow for managing Kubernetes resources declaratively.
data.code:
kubectl apply -f app.yaml
kubectl delete -f app.yaml
kubectl delete deployment nginx-deployment
kubectl delete pod bad-pod --grace-period=0

data.text: When something is wrong, these commands help you see what's happening inside the cluster.

rows: View pod logs; add `-f` to follow
View logs of a crashed container
Open an interactive shell in a running pod
See detailed resource status and events

data.title: Debugging a failing pod
data.content: Inspect logs and events to diagnose common pod issues.
data.code:
# Check pod status and events
kubectl describe pod my-pod

# View logs
kubectl logs my-pod
kubectl logs --previous my-pod

# Shell into the pod
kubectl exec -it my-pod -- /bin/sh

data.text: kubectl can output results in multiple formats. `-o wide` adds extra columns, `-o yaml` and `-o json` print full resource definitions. You can also use `jsonpath` expressions to extract specific fields.

data.title: Output formatting
data.content: Extract specific fields from kubectl output.
data.code:
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl get pod my-pod -o yaml
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion}'

data.title: kubectl shortcuts
data.text: You can alias `k=kubectl` and enable auto-completion with `source <(kubectl completion bash)`. Many operators also use `--dry-run=client -o yaml` to preview manifests before applying.

data.title: kubectl scavenger hunt
data.description: Practice the kubectl commands you have learned by exploring a live or local cluster.
steps: List all namespaces and identify the system namespaces.
Describe the kube-system namespace and note the running pods.
Get detailed output for one pod using `kubectl describe`.
Stream logs from a running pod using `kubectl logs -f`.
Use a label selector to list only pods with `app=nginx`.
Export one pod definition to YAML using `kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml`.
data.expectedOutcome: You can navigate any Kubernetes cluster using `get`, `describe`, `logs`, and label selectors.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `kubectl get` and `kubectl describe` to inspect resources at all levels.
Always apply manifests with `kubectl apply -f` and clean up with `kubectl delete`.
Use `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec` for debugging running pods.
Output flags like `-o wide` and `jsonpath` help you extract exactly what you need.
data.takeaway: Mastering kubectl is essential for operating Kubernetes clusters efficiently.
